Getting Oriented — What This System Is For

blocks.x: Every organ in this system exists to do one of four jobs: make an egg, move it, house a pregnancy, or feed the newborn. If you can say which job a structure serves, most of its anatomy stops being a list to memorise and starts making sense.

blocks.name: The female reproductive system
blocks.def: Made of internal organs — the paired ovaries, uterine (fallopian) tubes, uterus and vagina — plus the external genitalia (vulva): mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, vestibular bulb and the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands.

blocks.x: The four internal organs, and the job each one does

blocks.name: Ovaries
blocks.def: The factory. Produce ova (eggs) and the hormones estrogen and progesterone. Everything else in the system responds to what the ovary releases.

blocks.name: Uterine (fallopian) tubes
blocks.def: The corridor. Transport the oocyte and then the zygote, and are the usual site of fertilization. Note the tube does the catching — it is not attached to the ovary.

blocks.name: Uterus
blocks.def: The nursery. Houses and nourishes the developing embryo and fetus; the site of implantation. Its lining is rebuilt every month for this purpose.

blocks.name: Vagina
blocks.def: The passage. The birth canal, the route for menstrual flow, and receives the penis during coitus.

blocks.x: The one idea that ties the whole topic together

Nearly every structure here is built to cycle. Follicles mature and regress, the endometrium thickens and sheds, cervical mucus thins and thickens — all choreographed by four hormones: FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone. When you meet a new structure, ask "what does it look like early in the cycle, and what does it look like late?" That single question answers a large share of exam questions.

blocks.name: The numbers worth carrying
blocks.def: 2 ovaries, roughly 14 g each · uterine tube 10–12 cm long · average cycle 28 days · about 400 ova matured in an entire lifetime.

blocks.name: Vast oversupply, selective survival
blocks.def: A female fetus has about 5 million primordial oocytes at 3 months' gestation. By birth only about 1 million remain, and across a whole reproductive life only about 400 ever mature. Everything else is lost to atresia. Hold on to this arc: the system starts with a huge surplus and spends the rest of its life selecting.

blocks.x: Start with the outside and work inwards; the ovary is only a few layers deep and the exam questions almost always come from those layers in order.

blocks.name: Gross appearance
blocks.def: Almond-shaped, compact organs, roughly 3 cm long, 1.5–2 cm wide, 1 cm thick, about 14 g each, sitting within the pelvis.

blocks.name: Mesovarium
blocks.def: The fold of peritoneum that suspends the ovary from the broad ligament and carries its blood vessels in. When a question asks what the ovary is attached by, this is the answer.

blocks.x: The coverings, from outside in

blocks.name: 1. Germinal epithelium
blocks.def: The outermost covering — a simple cuboidal to squamous epithelium. The name is a historical mistake: it does not give rise to the germ cells. It matters clinically because it is torn and repaired at every ovulation.

blocks.name: 2. Tunica albuginea
blocks.def: A fibrous capsule of dense irregular collagenous connective tissue lying immediately beneath the germinal epithelium. Think of it as the ovary's tough white jacket.

blocks.name: 3. Cortex
blocks.def: The outer working zone, containing follicles at every stage of development embedded in stroma. This is where all the action of the ovarian cycle happens.

blocks.name: 4. Medulla
blocks.def: The inner core: loose connective tissue carrying large contorted blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves — the supply line. The boundary between cortex and medulla is indistinct, which is itself a favourite exam point.

blocks.x: What the ovary actually produces

blocks.name: Oogenesis
blocks.def: The production of gametes in the female. Developing gametes are called oocytes; the mature gamete is an ovum.

blocks.name: Estrogens
blocks.def: Drive growth and maturation of the internal and external sex organs, the female secondary sex characteristics, and breast development. Broadly, estrogen is the "build and grow" hormone.

blocks.name: Progesterone
blocks.def: Prepares the uterus for pregnancy and the mammary gland for lactation (lobular proliferation). Broadly, progesterone is the "prepare and maintain" hormone. The name itself says it: pro-gestation.

blocks.x: This is the single most examined sequence in the topic. Each stage is defined by two things: the shape of the cells around the oocyte, and whether a fluid cavity has appeared. Track those two features and the whole ladder falls into place.

blocks.name: Stage 1 — Primordial follicle
blocks.def: The earliest stage, first appearing in the 3rd month of fetal life. Found in the cortical stroma just beneath the tunica albuginea. A single layer of squamous (flat) follicle cells surrounds a large oocyte with a large nucleus and prominent nucleolus. Key feature: flat cells, one layer.

blocks.name: Stage 2 — Primary follicle (unilaminar)
blocks.def: The oocyte enlarges and the flat cells become cuboidal — still a single layer. The oocyte now secretes glycoproteins that form the zona pellucida between itself and the follicle cells. Key feature: cells change shape from flat to cuboidal.

blocks.name: Stage 3 — Primary follicle (multilaminar / late primary)
blocks.def: The follicle cells now stratify into several layers, together called the granulosa. Outside the basal lamina, stromal cells organise into the theca folliculi. Key feature: more than one layer.

blocks.name: Theca interna
blocks.def: The inner theca layer: vascularised, rich in LH receptors, and secretory — it produces androgens, which the granulosa cells then convert to estrogen. This division of labour is the classic "two-cell, two-gonadotrophin" idea.

blocks.name: Theca externa
blocks.def: The outer theca layer: smooth muscle and collagen — structural rather than hormonal.

blocks.name: Stage 4 — Secondary (antral) follicle
blocks.def: Once the granulosa reaches 6–12 cell layers, small fluid-filled spaces appear and merge into a single crescent-shaped cavity, the antrum. Key feature: the cavity appears. The oocyte reaches about 125 µm and then stops growing, held in check by oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) from the granulosa cells.

blocks.name: Liquor folliculi
blocks.def: The fluid filling the antrum — rich in hyaluronan, and containing enzymes, hormones, anticoagulants, electrolytes and nutrients. It is the medium the oocyte floats in.

blocks.name: Stage 5 — Graafian (mature) follicle
blocks.def: The antrum enlarges greatly and the follicle swells from about 0.2 mm to 10 mm or more. It contains the mature secondary oocyte, ready for release. Key feature: a huge antrum and a mound of cells holding the oocyte.

blocks.name: Cumulus oophorus
blocks.def: The mound of granulosa cells projecting into the antrum, on which the oocyte sits — literally the "egg-bearing hill".

blocks.name: Corona radiata
blocks.def: The innermost ring of granulosa cells that stays attached to the oocyte and leaves with it at ovulation. Cumulus stays behind; corona radiata travels — that contrast is commonly tested.

blocks.x: Two timing facts examiners like

blocks.name: How long development takes
blocks.def: Approximately 290 days for a recruited primordial follicle to become a fully grown secondary follicle. Follicle growth is a months-long process, not a monthly one.

blocks.name: Atresia
blocks.def: The loss of follicles by apoptosis of granulosa cells. It happens in large numbers during fetal life, early infancy and puberty. After puberty a group of follicles begins maturing each cycle, but normally only one completes the journey — the rest are wasted.

sections.title: The Zona Pellucida — Four Proteins, One Gatekeeper

blocks.x: The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat around the primary oocyte. Treat it as a security door: one protein lets the right visitor in, one holds the door together, and after entry the lock is destroyed so nobody else follows.

blocks.name: ZP1
blocks.def: Cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, holding the mesh together and thereby preventing extra sperm from binding.

blocks.name: ZP2
blocks.def: The secondary spermatozoa-binding protein — it holds on to sperm that have already begun the process.

blocks.name: ZP3
blocks.def: The one to remember: it permits sperm binding and triggers the acrosome reaction. If a question asks which zona protein is the primary sperm receptor, the answer is ZP3.

blocks.name: ZP4
blocks.def: Function currently unknown.

blocks.name: Ovastacin and the block to polyspermy
blocks.def: After fertilization the ovum secretes ovastacin, an enzyme that degrades ZP2. With ZP2 destroyed no further sperm can bind — this is the block to polyspermy, which prevents a lethal double fertilization.

blocks.x: After the follicle bursts, the leftover shell does not simply vanish — it converts, step by step, into an endocrine gland and then into a scar. Learn it as a four-stage story with a fork at the end.

blocks.name: Ovulation
blocks.def: Occurs in response to the LH surge. The secondary oocyte together with its corona radiata leaves the ruptured follicle. Note carefully: what is released is a secondary oocyte, not a fully mature ovum.

blocks.name: Corpus hemorrhagicum
blocks.def: The immediate remnant of the ruptured follicle. Blood enters the former antrum and clots; macrophages and connective tissue cells then clear the clot and debris. It is a transient structure — a bruise that is about to become a gland.

blocks.name: Corpus luteum
blocks.def: The "yellow body" that forms next, under the influence of estrogens, prolactin, LH, hCG and IGF-I/II. It is a genuine temporary endocrine gland.

blocks.name: Luteinization
blocks.def: The conversion itself: granulosa cells become granulosa luteal cells and theca interna cells become theca luteal cells. They enlarge, fill with lipid droplets (the raw material for steroid hormones) and a rich vascular network grows in. The cells that once fed the egg now become a hormone factory.

blocks.name: What the corpus luteum secretes
blocks.def: Mainly progesterone — which prepares the uterus for pregnancy — along with estrogens.

blocks.x: The fork in the road

blocks.name: No fertilization — corpus luteum of menstruation
blocks.def: Stays active only about 14 days, then degenerates (roughly 10–12 days after its peak). This fixed 14-day lifespan is exactly why the luteal phase is the constant part of the cycle.

blocks.name: Corpus albicans
blocks.def: The white scar the corpus luteum leaves behind. Over months it sinks deeper into the cortex. "Albicans" = white; "luteum" = yellow — the colour tells you which stage you are looking at down the microscope.

blocks.name: Fertilization occurs — corpus luteum of pregnancy
blocks.def: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum and maintains it for about 3 months, after which the placenta takes over steroid production. hCG is also what a pregnancy test detects.

blocks.x: The four luteal hormones and what each one does

blocks.name: Progesterone
blocks.def: The major hormone of the corpus luteum. Inhibits LH release (by suppressing LHRH) and promotes development of the uterine endometrium.

blocks.name: Estrogen
blocks.def: Inhibits FSH release (also by suppressing LHRH).

blocks.name: Relaxin
blocks.def: Facilitates parturition (childbirth) — it softens tissue in preparation for delivery.

blocks.name: Inhibin
blocks.def: Inhibits FSH synthesis and release in the pituitary and reduces hypothalamic LHRH content. The name is a gift: inhibin inhibits FSH.

blocks.x: Clinical correlates

blocks.name: Ovarian cancer
blocks.def: More than 70% of ovarian cancers arise from the surface (germinal) epithelium. The leading explanation is the repeated disruption and repair of that epithelium at every ovulation — more ovulations over a lifetime means more chances for a repair to go wrong.

blocks.name: Hormonal contraception
blocks.def: The pill, patch and ring contain synthetic estrogen/progestin. They work in three ways: prevent ovulation, prevent fertilization, and thicken cervical mucus so sperm cannot get through.

blocks.name: Mifepristone (RU-486)
blocks.def: Ends a pregnancy by blocking progesterone action — remove progesterone's support and the endometrium cannot sustain the pregnancy.

blocks.x: The tube has one job — get the oocyte from the ovary to the uterus, and host fertilization on the way. Its four parts, running medial to lateral, are best learned with their lengths attached, because the lengths are what get examined.

blocks.name: General features
blocks.def: Paired hollow muscular tubes, about 10–12 cm long and 0.5–1.2 cm wide, lying at the upper free border of the broad ligament (the mesosalpinx).

blocks.name: A detail that explains a lot
blocks.def: The tube runs toward the ovary but is not joined to it. Ova are released into the peritoneal cavity and must be caught. That is why the tube connects the uterine cavity to the peritoneal cavity — and why an egg (or an embryo) can occasionally end up in the wrong place.

blocks.x: The four parts, medial to lateral

blocks.name: 1. Intramural / interstitial (1 cm)
blocks.def: Embedded in the uterine wall, opening into the uterus at the superior-lateral angles. The narrowest, most protected segment.

blocks.name: 2. Isthmus (2.5–3 cm)
blocks.def: The constricted part medial to the ampulla — straight, narrow, with thicker walls than the ampulla.

blocks.name: 3. Ampulla (5 cm)
blocks.def: The longest and widest part, with a tortuous course. This is the usual site of fertilization, and therefore also the commonest site of an ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.name: 4. Infundibulum (1 cm)
blocks.def: The lateral, funnel-shaped end with the abdominal opening, fringed by finger-like fimbriae that sweep across the ovarian surface and guide the ovum into the tube.

blocks.x: Blood supply — split in a thirds pattern

blocks.name: Medial two-thirds
blocks.def: Supplied by the uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery.

blocks.name: Lateral one-third
blocks.def: Supplied by the ovarian artery, which comes directly from the abdominal aorta. Venous drainage goes to the pampiniform plexus of the ovary and the uterine veins.

blocks.x: The wall — three coats

blocks.name: Mucosa
blocks.def: Thrown into extensive longitudinal folds, which are greatest in the infundibulum and get smaller toward the uterus. More folds means more surface to catch and guide the egg.

blocks.name: Muscularis
blocks.def: Ill-defined inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle — it produces the peristaltic waves that move the oocyte along.

blocks.name: Serosa
blocks.def: Visceral peritoneum: simple squamous epithelium over thin connective tissue.

blocks.x: Two cell types, controlled by two hormones

blocks.name: Peg cells (secretory)
blocks.def: Secrete a nutrient-rich medium that nourishes spermatozoa and the pre-implantation embryo. Progesterone increases their number, so they predominate in the luteal phase — exactly when an embryo might be travelling through and needs feeding.

blocks.name: Ciliated cells
blocks.def: Their cilia beat mainly toward the uterine lumen, carrying the oocyte or embryo toward the uterus (sperm swim the other way). Estrogen increases their number and ciliary motion, so they are numerous in the follicular phase, when epithelial height is also greatest.

blocks.name: The regional pattern
blocks.def: Secretory cells increase toward the uterus; ciliated cells increase toward the infundibulum. It makes functional sense: you need sweeping where you catch the egg, and feeding where the embryo is heading.

blocks.x: Clinical notes

blocks.name: Ectopic pregnancy
blocks.def: The tube is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy, and the ampulla the commonest part — because that is where fertilization normally happens.

blocks.name: Salpingitis and sterility
blocks.def: Tubal blockage, often following inflammation (salpingitis), causes sterility — the sperm and egg simply cannot meet. Tubectomy is female sterilization performed on this principle deliberately.

sections.title: The Uterus — Shape, Position and Wall

blocks.name: General features
blocks.def: A muscular, hollow, pear-shaped organ, flattened front to back. In a woman who has never given birth (nulliparous) it measures about 8 × 5 × 3 cm, weighs 30–50 g, and has a cavity of only about 10 mL.

blocks.x: The four regions, top to bottom

blocks.name: Fundus
blocks.def: The rounded superior portion above the level of the tubal openings. This is the usual site of implantation.

blocks.name: Body (corpus)
blocks.def: The main part, containing the uterine cavity. It continues into the cervix at the internal os.

blocks.name: Isthmus
blocks.def: The constricted zone between body and cervix, corresponding to the internal os.

blocks.name: Cervix
blocks.def: The lower, barrel-shaped portion that opens into the vagina.

blocks.x: Normal position — two words that are easy to confuse

blocks.name: Anteverted (about 90°)
blocks.def: The cervix tilts forward relative to the vagina. Version = the angle between cervix and vagina.

blocks.name: Anteflexed (120–170°)
blocks.def: The body tilts forward relative to the cervix. Flexion = the angle between body and cervix. Remember it as: version is lower down, flexion is higher up.

blocks.name: Why this position matters
blocks.def: Being anteverted and anteflexed means that when intra-abdominal pressure rises (coughing, lifting), the uterus is pressed against the bladder rather than down the vagina — preventing it from bulging through, i.e. prolapse.

blocks.x: What holds it in place

blocks.name: Muscular support
blocks.def: The perineal body, the pelvic diaphragm, and the urogenital diaphragm — the floor the uterus rests upon.

blocks.name: Fibromuscular support
blocks.def: The uterosacral, cardinal (transverse cervical), pubocervical and round ligaments — the guy-ropes holding it in position.

blocks.x: The three layers of the uterine wall, outer to inner

blocks.name: Perimetrium
blocks.def: The outermost layer — visceral peritoneum. It is a serosa where the uterus bulges into the peritoneal cavity, and an adventitia where the surface is retroperitoneal.

blocks.name: Myometrium
blocks.def: The thick muscular middle layer: interlacing bundles of smooth muscle in three layers — inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal.

blocks.name: Stratum vasculare
blocks.def: The name for the middle circular myometrial layer, which is thick and richly vascularised — hence "vascular layer".

blocks.name: The myometrium in pregnancy
blocks.def: It undergoes both hypertrophy (cells enlarge) and hyperplasia (cells increase in number). Near term it develops gap junctions so that the whole muscle can contract as one coordinated unit during labour, triggered by oxytocin and prostaglandins. After delivery, estrogen falls and the smooth muscle cells undergo apoptosis, shrinking the uterus back down.

blocks.name: Endometrium
blocks.def: The mucosal lining: a simple columnar epithelium (secretory and ciliated cells) sitting on a gland-rich connective tissue stroma containing macrophages, leukocytes and simple tubular glands. Thickness swings from under 1 mm to about 7 mm across the cycle. This is the layer that implants an embryo, and the layer that is shed as a period.

sections.title: Endometrial Layers and Their Blood Supply

blocks.x: Almost everything about menstruation is explained by one design decision: the endometrium has two layers with two different blood supplies, and only one of them is disposable.

blocks.name: Functional layer (stratum functionalis)
blocks.def: The thick, superficial layer that is built up and shed every month. This is what appears as menstrual flow.

blocks.name: Basal layer (stratum basalis)
blocks.def: The deep layer, 1 mm or less, which is preserved during menstruation. Its glands are the seed stock that re-epithelialise the endometrium after shedding — which is why a period does not leave a permanent wound.

blocks.x: The arterial chain, in order

blocks.name: The route
blocks.def: Internal iliac artery → uterine artery → arcuate arteries (running within the myometrium) → radial branches → then the crucial split into spiral and straight arteries.

blocks.name: Spiral (coiled) arteries
blocks.def: Supply the functional layer and undergo cyclic change — they lengthen and coil as the layer thickens. Being coiled and hormone-sensitive is exactly what allows them to constrict and trigger shedding.

blocks.name: Straight arteries
blocks.def: Supply the basal layer and show no cyclic change — a permanent supply for the layer that must survive. That is why the basalis is spared while the functionalis dies.

blocks.x: Three phases, each defined by which hormone is in charge and what the glands look like. If you can state those two things, you can answer almost any cycle question.

blocks.name: Phase 1 — Menstrual phase (days 1–5)
blocks.def: Begins on the first day of bleeding, which is by convention day 1 of the cycle. Estrogen, progesterone, FSH and LH are all low.

blocks.name: The mechanism of menstruation
blocks.def: It is a vascular event, not simply a "collapse". Spiral arteries go into spasm: 2–3 days of vasoconstriction starve the functional layer, causing ischemia and necrosis. Then comes sudden vasodilation, which ruptures the weakened vessel walls, floods the stroma with blood and detaches the dead functional layer — producing the haemorrhagic discharge.

blocks.name: Phase 2 — Proliferative (follicular) phase (days 5–14)
blocks.def: Driven by rising estrogen from the growing follicles, and continuing until about one day after ovulation. The entire functional layer is rebuilt — glands, connective tissue and vessels all repair.

blocks.name: What the proliferative endometrium looks like
blocks.def: Glands are straight, simple columnar and narrow-lumened. Stromal cells divide, accumulate glycogen and enlarge. Coiled arteries extend about two-thirds of the way into the endometrium. By the end of the phase the endometrium is roughly 3 mm thick. Subdivided into early (5–7), mid (8–10) and late (11–14).

blocks.name: Phase 3 — Secretory (luteal / postovulatory) phase (days 15–28)
blocks.def: Begins 1–2 days after ovulation and is governed by progesterone from the corpus luteum. The endometrium is now being stocked and softened for a possible implantation.

blocks.name: What the secretory endometrium looks like
blocks.def: The endometrium thickens through oedema plus glandular secretion. Glands become coiled/corkscrew-shaped and their lumina fill with glycogen-rich secretion; cells accumulate glycogen basally. Coiled arteries extend further into the functional layer. By the end it is oedematous and about 6–7 mm thick. Subdivided into early (15–18, LH+1 to +4 — glandular changes), mid (19–23, LH+5 to +9 — stromal changes) and late (24–28, LH+10 to +14).

blocks.x: The quickest way to tell the two main phases apart

blocks.name: Straight versus coiled
blocks.def: Proliferative = estrogen = straight, narrow glands, ~3 mm. Secretory = progesterone = coiled, secretion-filled glands, ~6–7 mm. One phase builds the structure; the other stocks the pantry.

blocks.x: The ovarian cycle running in parallel

blocks.name: Follicular phase (days 1–13)
blocks.def: FSH begins follicle development. In the uterus, this overlaps the menstrual and proliferative phases.

blocks.name: Ovulation (day 14)
blocks.def: The LH surge causes release of the egg into the uterine tube.

blocks.name: Luteal phase (days 15–28)
blocks.def: The corpus luteum forms and produces estrogen, progesterone and inhibin. In the uterus, this is the secretory phase.

blocks.name: How the cycle resets
blocks.def: Without implantation: the corpus luteum degenerates into the corpus albicans, hormone levels fall, and menstruation plus a new round of follicular maturation begin. With implantation: hCG maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over.

blocks.x: Cycle calculations

blocks.name: Length of the cycle
blocks.def: Follicular phase + luteal phase. The luteal phase is fixed at about 14 days; it is the follicular phase that varies. So when a woman's cycle is longer or shorter than 28 days, it is the first half that has changed.

blocks.name: Chronological (calendar) date
blocks.def: (Current date − LMP) + 1. If the LMP fell in the previous month: (last day of previous month − LMP) + current date + 1.

blocks.name: Next menstrual period (NMP)
blocks.def: (LMP + average cycle length) − 1. If the LMP fell in the prior month: (LMP + average cycle length) − (last day of previous month + 1). LMP = last menstrual period.

blocks.x: The cervix — the odd one out

blocks.name: Two things the cervix does NOT have
blocks.def: It is not involved in menstruation and it lacks spiral arteries. Since spiral arteries are what drive shedding, no spiral arteries means no shedding — the two facts are really one fact.

blocks.name: Wall composition
blocks.def: Mainly dense collagenous connective tissue with elastic fibres and only a few smooth muscle cells. It is built to stay shut and hold a pregnancy in, so it is largely fibrous rather than muscular.

blocks.name: Two epithelia — and where they change
blocks.def: The endocervical canal is lined by simple columnar, mucus-secreting epithelium with scattered ciliated cells. The inferior portion, continuous with the vagina, is stratified squamous non-keratinized. The abrupt change between them is the transformation zone — clinically the site sampled by a smear.

blocks.name: Cervical glands
blocks.def: Branched glands secreting mucus. Their output increases about tenfold near ovulation, which thins the plug and facilitates sperm entry at precisely the moment it would be useful.

blocks.name: Mucus across the cycle
blocks.def: Thin at midcycle/ovulation (estrogen-driven) so sperm can swim through; thick and viscous during pregnancy, which hinders entry of sperm and microbes and protects the fetus.

blocks.name: Relaxin and cervical ripening
blocks.def: Before parturition, relaxin lyses collagen bundles, softening and dilating the cervix so it can open for delivery. Since the cervix is mostly collagen, dissolving collagen is exactly how you soften it.

blocks.x: The vagina

blocks.name: General features
blocks.def: A highly expansible fibromuscular tube, about 10 cm long, running from the vestibule to the cervix. It serves as the birth canal, the passage for menstrual flow, and receives the penis during coitus.

blocks.name: A commonly missed fact
blocks.def: The vagina has no glands anywhere along its length. All its lubrication comes from cervical secretion.

blocks.name: Mucosa
blocks.def: Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium over a fibroelastic lamina propria. Under estrogen the epithelium accumulates glycogen — greatest at ovulation.

blocks.name: Why vaginal pH is acidic
blocks.def: Resident bacteria convert that stored glycogen into lactic acid, lowering vaginal pH to about 3.5–4.0, which inhibits pathogens. It is a self-defending environment powered by a sugar the epithelium stores on estrogen's instruction.

blocks.name: Muscularis
blocks.def: Irregularly arranged smooth muscle — theoretically inner circular and outer longitudinal — interspersed with elastic fibres, which is what allows the enormous stretch required at delivery.

blocks.name: Adventitia
blocks.def: Fibroelastic connective tissue anchoring the vagina to surrounding structures.

blocks.x: Innervation — a clean two-thirds / one-third split

blocks.name: Upper two-thirds
blocks.def: Insensitive to pain, touch and temperature, but sensitive to stretch. Supplied by sympathetic (L1–L2) and parasympathetic (S2–S3) fibres.

blocks.name: Lower one-third (including the vaginal orifice)
blocks.def: Very sensitive to touch, supplied by the pudendal nerve via its inferior rectal and posterior labial branches. This split is why anaesthesia for the lower vagina targets the pudendal nerve.

blocks.x: Related structures

blocks.name: Fornix
blocks.def: The recess between cervix and vaginal wall. The posterior fornix is the deepest, is covered by the peritoneum of the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), and acts as a semen reservoir. Its relation to the pouch of Douglas is why it is used to access that space clinically.

blocks.name: Hymen
blocks.def: A thin, incomplete mucosal fold near the external orifice. After rupture its remnants are called hymenal caruncles.

blocks.name: Blood supply and lymphatics
blocks.def: Vaginal branches of the uterine and internal iliac arteries. Lymph: upper three-quarters → internal iliac nodes; lower quarter → superficial inguinal nodes. That difference matters for how tumours spread.

blocks.x: The vulva is best learned through its male homologues — nearly every structure has a counterpart, and remembering the pair means remembering both at once.

blocks.name: What the vulva includes
blocks.def: The mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, vestibular bulb and the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands. Its appearance changes across the lifespan — infancy, puberty, pregnancy and menopause.

blocks.name: Mons pubis
blocks.def: The fatty pad overlying the pubic symphysis, bearing pubic hair after puberty; contains adipose tissue.

blocks.name: Labia majora
blocks.def: The homologue of the male scrotum. Contain adipose tissue and large sebaceous follicles, and enclose the labia minora. The space between them is the pudendal cleft.

blocks.name: A useful clinical pattern
blocks.def: Hair-bearing skin (outer labia majora, mons pubis) is a common site of folliculitis and abscesses — because it has hair follicles to infect. Non-hair-bearing labia minora instead develop sebaceous cysts. The skin type predicts the lesion.

blocks.name: Vestibule
blocks.def: The space bounded by the labia minora, into which four things open: the vagina, the external urethra, the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands, and the para-urethral (Skene's) glands.

blocks.name: Clitoris
blocks.def: Erectile tissue homologous to the penis, divided into the glans, the body (two corpora cavernosa) and the crura. The glans is highly innervated and richly perfused, and is hooded by a fold of skin, the prepuce.

blocks.name: Bulbs of the vestibule
blocks.def: Two masses of erectile tissue around the vaginal opening, equivalent to the male corpus spongiosum. They contact Bartholin's glands posteriorly and the clitoris anteriorly.

blocks.x: The glands of the vulva

blocks.name: Para-urethral (Skene's) glands
blocks.def: Homologous to the prostate. They discharge into the urethra near its external opening, lubricating it and providing antimicrobial defence against urinary tract infections. They secrete mucus during sexual activity, may be the source of female ejaculation (their fluid contains PSA and high glucose/fructose), and are thought to underlie the G-spot.

blocks.name: Greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands
blocks.def: Two bean-shaped glands posterior to the vestibular bulb, homologous to the male bulbourethral glands. Each opens by a single duct between the labium minus and the hymen — typically at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions. They secrete mucus during arousal to lubricate the vaginal opening. Blockage or infection causes Bartholinitis or a Bartholin's abscess.

blocks.name: Lesser vestibular glands
blocks.def: Very small mucous glands opening between the urethral and vaginal openings.

blocks.name: Blood supply
blocks.def: The internal and external pudendal arteries.

blocks.name: What it actually is
blocks.def: A modified sweat gland whose function is to secrete milk to nourish an infant. Non-lactating weight 150–225 g; a lactating breast may exceed 500 g.

blocks.x: Where it sits

blocks.name: Position
blocks.def: In the subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) lying over pectoralis major and serratus anterior. It is not part of the muscle — it rests on it.

blocks.name: Retromammary space
blocks.def: A layer of loose areolar tissue separating the breast from the deep fascia, which is what allows the breast to move freely over the muscle. Loss of that mobility is a warning sign, because a tumour fixing to deeper tissue tethers the breast.

blocks.name: Extent
blocks.def: From the 2nd to the 6th ribs, and from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line.

blocks.name: Axillary tail (of Spence)
blocks.def: An extension of breast tissue from the upper lateral quadrant toward the axilla. The upper lateral quadrant is the site of roughly 50% of breast cancers — which is why quadrant description matters clinically.

blocks.x: Internal architecture

blocks.name: Lobes and ducts
blocks.def: 15–20 lobes of glandular tissue separated by radiating fibrous septa. Each lobe drains by a lactiferous duct opening onto the nipple tip.

blocks.name: Lactiferous sinus
blocks.def: The enlargement of the duct just before the nipple, which acts as a reservoir for milk during lactation.

blocks.name: Suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments
blocks.def: Fibrous bands connecting the dermis to the deep fascia, maintaining the breast's shape in youth. With age-related atrophy they slacken, allowing ptosis (drooping). When a tumour pulls on them it causes skin dimpling.

blocks.x: Nipple and areola

blocks.name: Nipple
blocks.def: The projection containing the lactiferous ducts and their orifices for milk delivery.

blocks.name: Areola and the glands of Montgomery
blocks.def: The pigmented skin patch around the nipple, containing areolar (Montgomery) glands — sebaceous glands producing an oily secretion that lubricates and protects the nipple and reduces cracking during nursing. They raise small bumps, the tubercles of Montgomery, which become especially prominent in pregnancy.

blocks.name: Blood supply
blocks.def: Mainly the lateral thoracic artery, with contributions from the internal thoracic, posterior intercostal and thoracoacromial arteries.

blocks.name: Innervation
blocks.def: The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of T2–T6.

blocks.x: How the breast changes through pregnancy and lactation

There is one trend running through all four stages: glandular tissue increases while connective tissue proportionally decreases. If you remember the direction of travel, you can reconstruct any stage.

blocks.name: 1. Resting (non-pregnant) breast
blocks.def: Abundant connective tissue with comparatively few glandular elements.

blocks.name: 2. Early pregnancy
blocks.def: Glandular elements increase; connective tissue proportionally decreases.

blocks.name: 3. Late pregnancy
blocks.def: Glandular epithelium prepares for lactation: alveoli enlarge and some already contain secretory product. Intralobular connective tissue decreases relative to interlobular. Myoepithelial cells surround the alveoli and lactiferous ducts become prominent — but milk secretion only begins after birth.

blocks.name: 4. Lactating breast
blocks.def: Large numbers of milk-filled alveoli with irregular branching, and further reduction of interlobular connective tissue. Not all alveoli are in the same secretory state at once — a classic histology observation.

blocks.name: Myoepithelial cells
blocks.def: Contractile cells wrapped around the alveoli; they squeeze milk into the ducts during the let-down reflex.

blocks.x: Developmental anomalies — learn them as a pair of pairs

blocks.name: Polymastia and polythelia
blocks.def: Poly- = extra. Polymastia = more than one pair of breasts; polythelia = more than one pair of nipples.

blocks.name: Amastia and athelia
blocks.def: A- = absent. Amastia = absence of breasts; athelia = absence of nipples. Pair the roots: mast = breast, thel = nipple.

sections.title: Watch it explained — The Noted Anatomist

blocks.x: The Noted Anatomist is a series of about 120 anatomy tutorials (3–35 minutes each) created by Dr. David A. Morton, PhD, professor of anatomy at the University of Utah School of Medicine. He teaches anatomy to medical, dental, PA, PT and OT students, and the series includes the female and male reproductive systems alongside the locomotor system, neuroanatomy, cardiovascular, digestive and abdominal wall topics.
The videos are organised by subject on the channel's playlists page, so the female reproductive and pelvis playlists are the ones to open alongside this guide.

blocks.name: 🎬 Channel home & playlists
blocks.def: youtube.com/channel/UCe9lb3da4XAnN7v3ciTyquQ — open the Playlists tab and choose the reproductive system / pelvis series.

blocks.name: 💡 How to use them with this guide
blocks.def: Read a section here first — for example follicular development or the layers of the uterine wall — then watch the matching tutorial. Seeing the structures rotated and dissected on screen fixes the spatial relationships that text alone struggles to convey.

blocks.x: Note: these tutorials are hosted on YouTube by their creator and are not part of this offline file, so you will need an internet connection to watch them.
